## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** The Carnot efficiency bound η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot (both in kelvin) is the maximum
  possible thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency of **any** heat engine — any working fluid,
  any cycle architecture, any equipment quality — operating between two fixed-temperature
  reservoirs; no engineering refinement can exceed it. — source: the Second Law of
  Thermodynamics (Kelvin–Planck/Clausius statements) via Carnot's theorem; standard engineering
  thermodynamics (e.g., Cengel & Boles, *Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach*, ch. on the
  Carnot cycle). This is a mathematical theorem derived from the Second Law, not an empirical
  measurement, so it passes the irreducibility test directly — it bottoms out at a physical law
  and is not reducible further.

- **GT-2** The Curzon–Ahlborn (endoreversible) efficiency η_CA = 1 − √(T_cold/T_hot) is the
  efficiency of an *idealized endoreversible* heat engine (internally reversible, but coupled to
  its reservoirs through finite-rate, irreversible heat exchange) operating **at the power output
  that maximizes power**, not the efficiency that maximizes efficiency — source: Curzon & Ahlborn
  (1975), "Efficiency of a Carnot engine at maximum power output," *Am. J. Phys.* 43(1); the same
  result was derived earlier by Chambadal (1957) and Novikov (1957). This is also a theorem
  within a specific, named engine model (reversible engine + finite-rate coupling, operated for
  maximum power), not a measurement — it bottoms out at a mathematical derivation from a stated
  model and is not reducible further, but note what it is and is not a bound *on*: it bounds
  engines tuned for maximum power density, not engines tuned for maximum efficiency, and a real
  plant in the second category can exceed it (see Assumptions §2 and chain C1).

- **GT-3** T [K] = T [°C] + 273.15 — source: SI definition of the kelvin relative to the degree
  Celsius. A definition, not a measurement; irreducible by construction.

- **GT-4** At Solar Two (the 10 MWe molten-salt power-tower demonstration plant near Barstow,
  CA, operated 1996–1999), hot salt was pumped "from the hot-salt sump (at 565°C)... through the
  shell side of the superheater, through the tube bundle in the kettle evaporator, and finally
  through the shell side of the preheater, where it returned to the cold salt storage tank at
  290°C" — source: Pacheco (ed.), *Final Test and Evaluation Results from the Solar Two Project*,
  Sandia SAND2002-0120 (OSTI 793226), §5.1; read-at-source: quoted verbatim from the extracted
  report text (the sentence spanning the SGS description). 565 °C hot-tank / 290 °C cold-tank is
  the reference operating window used across Solar-Salt (NaNO₃/KNO₃) commercial towers of this
  design generation, including the Crescent Dunes-class design basis used in GT-5/GT-6 below.
  T_hot = 565 °C + 273.15 ≈ **838 K**.

- **GT-5** For a 565 °C-salt molten-salt power tower Rankine power block, Sandia's design-point
  heat-balance study specifies a condenser design pressure of **0.087 bar for wet-cooled
  condensing** (saturation temperature ≈ 43 °C ≈ **316 K**) and **0.17 bar for dry-cooled
  condensing**, the latter sized for a hottest-time-of-year ambient of 42.8 °C and a design
  initial-temperature-difference (ITD) of 14 °C, giving a condenser saturation temperature ≈
  56.8 °C ≈ **330 K** — source: Kolb, *An Evaluation of Possible Next-Generation High Temperature
  Molten-Salt Power Towers*, Sandia SAND2011-9320 (OSTI 1035342), p. 33 ("Steam conditions...
  Condenser pressure (bar)... Wet-cooled condenser 0.087... Dry-cooled condenser 0.17") and p. 40
  ("the design condition was the hottest time of the year (42.8 °C), a condenser design pressure
  of 0.17 bar... and a design initial-temperature difference (ITD) of 14 °C"); read-at-source:
  quoted verbatim from the extracted report text.

- **GT-6** For the same study, design-point **gross** Rankine cycle efficiency (thermal energy
  into the steam generator → gross electric out) is tabulated for three steam conditions at the
  two condenser options above:

  | Steam condition | Pressure/temperature | Wet-cooled gross η | Dry-cooled gross η |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Subcritical (current practice) | 125 bar / 537 °C | 43.0% | 41.2% |
  | Supercritical | 301 bar / 591 °C | 48.4% | 46.8% |
  | Ultrasupercritical | 331 bar / 630 °C | 49.6% | 48.0% |

  — source: Kolb, SAND2011-9320 (OSTI 1035342), p. 33 table and confirmed against the individual
  heat-balance figures for each case (e.g., "0.430 gross cycle efficiency" for subcritical/wet,
  "0.412" for subcritical/dry, "0.496" for ultrasupercritical/wet, "0.480" for
  ultrasupercritical/dry); read-at-source: quoted/matched verbatim from the extracted report
  text. The subcritical row is the technology in commercial deployment today (the live-steam
  temperature of 537 °C sits ≈28 °C below the 565 °C salt temperature — the heat-exchanger
  approach gap named in the problem). Independently, a 2012 DOE SunShot program fact sheet gives
  "approximately 41%" for the dry-cooled case (GT-8), corroborating the 41.2% figure from a
  separate document.

- **GT-7** At Solar Two, the steam generator/turbine/generator train ("EPGS") achieved a measured
  steady-state thermal-to-**gross**-electric conversion efficiency of **34.1% at full load**
  (34±0.3% average across the test program, Table 6-1), matching Bechtel Group's own prediction
  for that specific hardware, against a **commercial-plant prediction of 42%** for the same row
  in the same table. The report states the reason directly: "the Rankine turbine was not a
  reheat design, its efficiency was limited to about 34%. Newer turbine designs that incorporate
  reheat have gross efficiencies greater than [42%]" and "[the turbine] efficiency was limited to
  34%. Larger steam turbines that have reheat will be more efficient, e.g., will reach 42%." The
  turbine was a non-reheat unit refurbished from the 1980s-vintage Solar One project, rated 12.8
  MWe gross, and was itself limited to a 510 °C steam inlet temperature even though the steam
  generator was designed to supply 535 °C steam. The same table gives the whole-plant "Overall
  Peak Efficiency" (the product of collection efficiency × EPGS efficiency × parasitics) as
  **13±0.4% measured against 22% predicted** for a commercial plant — a different, larger
  quantity than the power-block efficiency, kept separate here per the "basis caveat" failure
  mode this technique warns against. — source: Pacheco (ed.), SAND2002-0120 (OSTI 793226), §5.1
  ("thermal-to-gross electric conversion efficiency was 34.1% at full load"), §6.1 Table 6-1, and
  §6.1.8 text; read-at-source: all figures quoted/matched verbatim from the extracted report
  text (Table 6-1, rows H and J; narrative at the EPGS and non-reheat-turbine passages).

- **GT-8** A 2012 U.S. DOE SunShot CSP R&D program fact sheet ("10-MW Supercritical-CO2 Turbine,"
  DOE/GO-102012-3667, September 2012, NREL project led by Craig Turchi) states: "Current
  state-of-the-art, molten-salt power towers have an operating limit of approximately 565°C. When
  combined with a dry-cooled steam Rankine power cycle, these systems have a thermal-to-electric
  conversion efficiency of approximately 41%," and states the program's goal as validating an
  sCO₂ turbine toward "high-efficiency power cycles that exceed 50% net thermal-to-electric
  conversion efficiency." — source: DOE/NREL SunShot CSP R&D fact sheet, energy.gov (SunShot CSP
  R&D 2012 program materials); read-at-source: the fact sheet page was fetched and read directly
  (quoted verbatim above).

- **GT-9** The same Sandia design study finds that raising receiver/hot-salt temperature from
  565 °C to 650 °C (enabling supercritical and then ultrasupercritical steam, GT-6) reduces
  levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) by roughly 8%, and that "most of that benefit can be
  achieved by raising the temperature to only 600 °C." — source: Kolb, SAND2011-9320 (OSTI
  1035342), Executive Summary; read-at-source: quoted/matched verbatim from the extracted report
  text.

- **GT-10?** DOE's "Generation 3" (Gen3) CSP program's Liquid Pathway design concept uses a
  sodium-cooled receiver operating near 740 °C, transferring heat through a liquid–liquid heat
  exchanger into a two-tank molten-chloride-salt storage system, which in turn supplies a
  supercritical-CO₂ (sCO₂) Brayton power cycle, because conventional nitrate salts are not
  chemically stable at these temperatures (GT-11?) — cited to: NREL, "CSP Gen3: Liquid-Phase
  Pathway to SunShot" (research-hub.nrel.gov) and the associated DOE Gen3 executive-summary PDF;
  reported-by-delegate: this analysis read a WebSearch summary of these pages, not the source
  documents themselves.

- **GT-11?** Nitrate-based heat-transfer/storage salts (the Solar-Salt family used at 290–565 °C
  in GT-4) are not thermally stable above roughly 600–620 °C, which is the chemical reason — not
  a cost or convention reason — that the current commercial technology generation is capped near
  565 °C and that reaching higher hot-reservoir temperatures requires a different salt chemistry
  (chloride salts) — cited to: a 2025 paper on ternary molten-chloride-salt (MgCl₂–KCl–NaCl)
  corrosion/creep behavior, surfaced via WebSearch; reported-by-delegate: cited source not opened
  by this analysis.

- **GT-12?** The Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project (SolarReserve, Tonopah, NV; 110 MW
  nameplate; operated intermittently 2015–2019) ran its hot salt tank "at almost 600 °C"
  against a 280 °C cold-tank base temperature, with roughly ten hours of thermal storage —
  source: Wikipedia, "Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project," infobox and body text; read-at-source
  for the Wikipedia page's own wording (quoted above), but **unverified as a fact about the
  plant**: other secondary sources (NREL project profiles, trade press) describe Crescent Dunes
  as a 565 °C-class design consistent with GT-4–GT-6, i.e. roughly 30–35 °C below the Wikipedia
  figure, and this analysis could not reach either primary engineering documentation (NREL's own
  SolarPACES project page returned a DNS failure when fetched) or a measured gross/net cycle
  efficiency for this specific plant. The hot-tank temperature and the efficiency gap this
  analysis would need to say anything quantitative about Crescent Dunes specifically are both
  flagged unresolved.

- **GT-13** At Solar Two, the ratio of net electrical output to gross EPGS output ("Parasitics")
  was measured at **87±0.4%** (i.e., ≈13% parasitic loss: salt pumps, feedwater pumps, cooling
  system, controls, BOP), against a **93%** (≈7% loss) commercial-plant prediction in the same
  table row — source: Pacheco (ed.), SAND2002-0120 (OSTI 793226), Table 6-1, row I; read-at-source:
  quoted/matched verbatim from the extracted report text.

- **GT-14?** The Gemasolar Thermosolar Plant (Torresol Energy, Fuentes de Andalucía, Spain;
  operational since 2011) has a 19.9 MW nameplate turbine and a measured capacity factor of
  45.9%, with roughly 15 hours of molten-salt thermal storage — source: Wikipedia, "Gemasolar
  Thermosolar Plant," infobox; read-at-source for the nameplate and capacity-factor figures
  (quoted/matched directly from the fetched page). The turbine is additionally reported elsewhere
  as a Siemens SST-600 two-cylinder **reheat** design (SAM/EPRI technical case documentation,
  surfaced via WebSearch) — **reported-by-delegate** for the reheat-configuration detail
  specifically: the SAM/EPRI documents themselves were not opened by this analysis (both
  sam.nrel.gov fetch attempts failed with a DNS error). No measured or design-point gross/net
  cycle efficiency for Gemasolar was located by this analysis.

  the reference operating window used across Solar-Salt (NaNO₃/KNO₃) commercial towers of this
  design generation, including the Crescent Dunes-class design basis used in GT-5/GT-6 below.
  T_hot = 565 °C + 273.15 ≈ **838 K**.

  heat-balance study specifies a condenser design pressure of **0.087 bar for wet-cooled
  condensing** (saturation temperature ≈ 43 °C ≈ **316 K**) and **0.17 bar for dry-cooled
  condensing**, the latter sized for a hottest-time-of-year ambient of 42.8 °C and a design
  initial-temperature-difference (ITD) of 14 °C, giving a condenser saturation temperature ≈
  56.8 °C ≈ **330 K** — source: Kolb, *An Evaluation of Possible Next-Generation High Temperature
  Molten-Salt Power Towers*, Sandia SAND2011-9320 (OSTI 1035342), p. 33 ("Steam conditions...
  Condenser pressure (bar)... Wet-cooled condenser 0.087... Dry-cooled condenser 0.17") and p. 40
  ("the design condition was the hottest time of the year (42.8 °C), a condenser design pressure
  of 0.17 bar... and a design initial-temperature difference (ITD) of 14 °C"); read-at-source:
  quoted verbatim from the extracted report text.

  into the steam generator → gross electric out) is tabulated for three steam conditions at the
  two condenser options above:

  | Steam condition | Pressure/temperature | Wet-cooled gross η | Dry-cooled gross η |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Subcritical (current practice) | 125 bar / 537 °C | 43.0% | 41.2% |
  | Supercritical | 301 bar / 591 °C | 48.4% | 46.8% |
  | Ultrasupercritical | 331 bar / 630 °C | 49.6% | 48.0% |

  — source: Kolb, SAND2011-9320 (OSTI 1035342), p. 33 table and confirmed against the individual
  heat-balance figures for each case (e.g., "0.430 gross cycle efficiency" for subcritical/wet,
  "0.412" for subcritical/dry, "0.496" for ultrasupercritical/wet, "0.480" for
  ultrasupercritical/dry); read-at-source: quoted/matched verbatim from the extracted report
  text. The subcritical row is the technology in commercial deployment today (the live-steam
  temperature of 537 °C sits ≈28 °C below the 565 °C salt temperature — the heat-exchanger

  "approximately 41%" for the dry-cooled case (GT-8), corroborating the 41.2% figure from a
  separate document.

  for that specific hardware, against a **commercial-plant prediction of 42%** for the same row
  in the same table. The report states the reason directly: "the Rankine turbine was not a
  reheat design, its efficiency was limited to about 34%. Newer turbine designs that incorporate
  reheat have gross efficiencies greater than [42%]" and "[the turbine] efficiency was limited to
  34%. Larger steam turbines that have reheat will be more efficient, e.g., will reach 42%." The
  turbine was a non-reheat unit refurbished from the 1980s-vintage Solar One project, rated 12.8

  generator was designed to supply 535 °C steam. The same table gives the whole-plant "Overall
  Peak Efficiency" (the product of collection efficiency × EPGS efficiency × parasitics) as
  **13±0.4% measured against 22% predicted** for a commercial plant — a different, larger

  mode this technique warns against. — source: Pacheco (ed.), SAND2002-0120 (OSTI 793226), §5.1

  state-of-the-art, molten-salt power towers have an operating limit of approximately 565°C. When
  combined with a dry-cooled steam Rankine power cycle, these systems have a thermal-to-electric
  conversion efficiency of approximately 41%," and states the program's goal as validating an
  sCO₂ turbine toward "high-efficiency power cycles that exceed 50% net thermal-to-electric
  conversion efficiency." — source: DOE/NREL SunShot CSP R&D fact sheet, energy.gov (SunShot CSP

  achieved by raising the temperature to only 600 °C." — source: Kolb, SAND2011-9320 (OSTI

python3 -I -c "
import math
Th=838.0
Tc_tank=563.0
T0_wet=316.0
T0_dry=330.0

def carnot(T0,Th):
    return 1-T0/Th

def ca(T0,Th):
    return 1-math.sqrt(T0/Th)

def exergy_ceiling(T0, Th, Tc_tank):
    return 1 - T0*math.log(Th/Tc_tank)/(Th-Tc_tank)

print('Carnot naive wet', carnot(T0_wet,Th))
print('Carnot naive dry', carnot(T0_dry,Th))
print('CA wet', ca(T0_wet,Th))
print('CA dry', ca(T0_dry,Th))
print('Exergy ceiling wet', exergy_ceiling(T0_wet,Th,Tc_tank))
print('Exergy ceiling dry', exergy_ceiling(T0_dry,Th,Tc_tank))

# ambient-only idealization
print('Carnot ambient 298K', carnot(298.0,Th))
print('Carnot ambient 313K', carnot(313.0,Th))

# 650C case
Th650=923.0
print('Carnot naive wet 650C', carnot(T0_wet,Th650))
print('Exergy ceiling wet 650C (assume same Tc_tank=563K)', exergy_ceiling(T0_wet,Th650,Tc_tank))

# gaps
design_wet=0.430
design_dry=0.412
usc_wet=0.496

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: The defensible law-permitted ceiling is the exergy-correct bound for a non-isothermal salt source (≈54.3% wet-cooled / ≈52.3% dry-cooled), not the naive single-reservoir Carnot figure (≈62.3%/60.6%) and not the Curzon-Ahlborn figure (≈38.6%/37.3%, which is not a ceiling at all)

GT-1 (Carnot bound, any heat engine between two reservoirs) + GT-2 (Curzon-Ahlborn, max-power endoreversible engine) + GT-3 (K = °C + 273.15) + GT-4 (hot salt 565 °C ≈ 838 K, cold-tank return 290 °C ≈ 563 K) + GT-5 (condenser design temperatures 316 K wet / 330 K dry) + GT-6 (design-point gross cycle efficiency 43.0% wet / 41.2% dry) + GT-15 (exergy-correct efficiency ceiling for a cooling, non-isothermal stream)
→ The salt loop, not the condenser, is being asked to stand in for "the hot reservoir," so the first question is which temperature pair the Second Law actually constrains here: the condenser is where the cycle rejects heat, while the salt only ever delivers it, so the cold tank is never a candidate cold reservoir *[Assumes: A-1]*
→ Substituting T_hot = 838 K and each T_cold from GT-5 into GT-1's single-reservoir formula gives a naive Carnot ceiling of 62.3% wet-cooled and 60.6% dry-cooled — a valid upper bound, since no real cycle anywhere in GT-6 or GT-7 exceeds it, but one that silently treats the 565 °C salt as an isothermal reservoir
→ The salt is not isothermal: GT-4 establishes that it cools from 838 K to 563 K while delivering the heat GT-6's efficiency figures are computed against, so GT-1's formula is evaluated at the wrong idealization for this specific heat source *[Assumes: A-2]*
→ Substituting T₁ = 838 K, T₂ = 563 K and each T₀ from GT-5 into GT-15's stream-exergy formula gives the correct ideal ceiling on the same Q-basis as GT-6: 54.3% wet-cooled and 52.3% dry-cooled, roughly 8 points below the naive Carnot figure
→ Substituting the same reservoir pair into GT-2's Curzon-Ahlborn formula gives 38.6% wet-cooled and 37.3% dry-cooled, both of which GT-6's real design-point gross efficiency (43.0%/41.2%) already exceeds *[Assumes: A-3]*
→ A ceiling that real, already-operating equipment exceeds is not a ceiling on that equipment, so Curzon-Ahlborn is ruled out as the law-permitted bound for an efficiency-tuned plant, leaving the GT-15 exergy-correct figure as the tightest ceiling no real design in GT-6 or measurement in GT-7 ever exceeds
→ For reference against the question's own suggested cold-reservoir range, using bare ambient temperatures of 298 K and 313 K directly in GT-1 (the zero-condenser-approach idealization, not a physically realized cold reservoir) gives 64.4% and 62.6% respectively — both looser than even the naive Carnot figure, because they additionally assume away the condenser's own finite approach

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2, GT-3, GT-4, GT-5, GT-6, GT-15 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — downgraded on the Inference axis, not the Inputs axis: every head identifier is an unsuffixed, read-at-source ground truth, but three hops rest on stated premises (A-1, A-2, A-3) about how to read the reservoir pair and which bound is physically applicable. Each premise's failure is priced rather than merely flagged: A-1's failure (treating the cold tank as the sink) is directly falsified by GT-6 exceeding the resulting 32.8% figure; A-3's failure (treating CA as binding) is directly falsified by GT-6 exceeding the CA value; A-2's failure (treating single-reservoir Carnot as already correct) would not falsify anything observable — it would just mean the naive 62.3%/60.6% figures stand uncorrected, which is the live rival this chain is written to rule out, and it is ruled out by direct derivation (GT-15 reduces to GT-1 in the isothermal limit, confirming GT-15 is the more general, strictly tighter result, not a competing one). No input is `?`-marked, so D-07 does not apply; the downgrade is Inference-axis only, with the rival reading (naive Carnot as the ceiling) explicitly named and settled here rather than left open.

---

### Conclusion C2: Current practice sits roughly 11 points below the correct gross-basis ceiling and roughly 14–16 points below it on a net-plant basis; plant-specific figures for Crescent Dunes and Gemasolar are genuinely unresolved rather than merely unstated

GT-6 (design-point gross efficiency 43.0% wet / 41.2% dry) + GT-7 (Solar Two measured 34.1% gross, non-reheat-limited; commercial prediction 42%) + GT-13 (parasitic retention 87% achieved / 93% commercial-predicted) + C1 (exergy-correct ceiling 54.3% wet / 52.3% dry)
→ Current commercial-generation design practice for a 565 °C subcritical molten-salt tower is 43.0% gross wet-cooled / 41.2% gross dry-cooled (GT-6), independently corroborated by a separate DOE SunShot document's "approximately 41%" dry-cooled figure (GT-8)
→ The only *measured* thermal-to-electric figure at these exact reservoir conditions is Solar Two's 34.1% gross, but that number is not representative of current commercial practice: its own test report attributes the shortfall to a non-reheat turbine refurbished from 1980s hardware, not to any shortfall of the technology class, and the same report's commercial-plant prediction (42%) is consistent with GT-6's 41.2–43.0% design figures *[Assumes: A-5]*
→ Applying GT-13's measured parasitic-retention ratio to GT-6's dry-cooled gross figure as a Fermi-style estimate — not a citation — brackets net plant electrical efficiency at roughly 35.8% (13% parasitic loss, as measured) to 38.3% (7% loss, as commercially predicted) *[Assumes: A-7]*
→ Against C1's exergy-correct ceiling, the gross-basis gap is 54.3% − 43.0% = 11.3 points wet-cooled and 52.3% − 41.2% = 11.1 points dry-cooled (≈21% relative), while the net-basis gap is 52.3% − 38.3% = 14.0 points at best and 52.3% − 35.8% = 16.5 points at worst (≈27–31% relative)
→ Had the naive single-reservoir Carnot figure from C1 been used instead of the exergy-correct one, the same arithmetic would report a gross gap of ≈19.3–19.4 points and a net gap of ≈22–25 points — roughly 8 points larger at every basis — so misidentifying the ceiling, not any property of the plant, would account for nearly half of the apparently "missing" efficiency
→ No measured or design-point gross/net cycle efficiency for either Crescent Dunes (110 MW, operated 2015–2019) or Gemasolar (19.9 MW, operating since 2011) was located by this analysis, and Crescent Dunes' own hot-tank temperature is reported inconsistently across sources by roughly 30–35 °C *[Assumes: A-6]*, so neither plant can be placed on the gap bracket above with any defensible precision — this is reported as a genuine data gap, not estimated past it

A-5 and A-6 are similarly named rather than resolved: A-5's failure would mean GT-6 overstates real achieved practice, which would *widen* this chain's gap rather than narrow it, so the conclusion's direction is robust to it; A-6's failure is already priced as the explicit "genuine data gap" stated in the chain's last hop rather than papered over.

48:---

7	→ Substituting T_hot = 838 K and each T_cold from GT-5 into GT-1's single-reservoir formula gives a naive Carnot ceiling of 62.3% wet-cooled and 60.6% dry-cooled — a valid upper bound, since no real cycle anywhere in GT-6 or GT-7 exceeds it, but one that silently treats the 565 °C salt as an isothermal reservoir
8	→ The salt is not isothermal: GT-4 establishes that it cools from 838 K to 563 K while delivering the heat GT-6's efficiency figures are computed against, so GT-1's formula is evaluated at the wrong idealization for this specific heat source *[Assumes: A-2]*
9	→ Substituting T₁ = 838 K, T₂ = 563 K and each T₀ from GT-5 into GT-15's stream-exergy formula gives the correct ideal ceiling on the same Q-basis as GT-6: 54.3% wet-cooled and 52.3% dry-cooled, roughly 8 points below the naive Carnot figure
10	→ Substituting the same reservoir pair into GT-2's Curzon-Ahlborn formula gives 38.6% wet-cooled and 37.3% dry-cooled, both of which GT-6's real design-point gross efficiency (43.0%/41.2%) already exceeds *[Assumes: A-3]*
11	→ A ceiling that real, already-operating equipment exceeds is not a ceiling on that equipment, so Curzon-Ahlborn is ruled out as the law-permitted bound for an efficiency-tuned plant, leaving the GT-15 exergy-correct figure as the tightest ceiling no real design in GT-6 or measurement in GT-7 ever exceeds
12	→ For reference against the question's own suggested cold-reservoir range, using bare ambient temperatures of 298 K and 313 K directly in GT-1 (the zero-condenser-approach idealization, not a physically realized cold reservoir) gives 64.4% and 62.6% respectively — both looser than even the naive Carnot figure, because they additionally assume away the condenser's own finite approach

F=".first-principles/analysis-20261011T040155Z.md" && cat >> "$F" <<'FP_EOF'
## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: The 290 °C cold salt tank as the cold reservoir

**What was tried:** Computing η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot using the two salt-tank temperatures
directly (565 °C hot tank, 290 °C cold tank) as the reservoir pair, since both are well-sourced,
round, and salient numbers (GT-4).

**Why abandoned:** The cold tank is the return leg of the heat *source* loop, not a heat sink —
nothing in the plant rejects waste heat at 290 °C. The arithmetic is well-formed (1 − 563/838 =
32.8%) but the result is not a ceiling on the actual machine: GT-6's real, operating design
practice (43.0% gross) already exceeds it. A bound real equipment exceeds has the wrong reservoir
pair, not a measurement error — this is the decisive test, and this framing fails it.

**What it ruled out:** Any later re-derivation that reaches for the tank pair because both
numbers are salt-side and convenient. The correct cold reservoir is always the point where the
*cycle* rejects heat (chain C1), never a temperature internal to the heat-delivery loop, however
tempting its availability.

### Dead End: Curzon-Ahlborn as the "more realistic" law-permitted ceiling

**What was tried:** Using η_CA = 1 − √(T_cold/T_hot) as the ceiling instead of (or alongside)
Carnot, on the reasoning offered in the question itself — that it "accounts for the unavoidable
finite-rate heat transfer needed to deliver nonzero power" and so is a tighter, more physically
honest bound than the classical, zero-power-limit Carnot figure.

**Why abandoned:** Curzon-Ahlborn is the efficiency of one specific, named engine model —
internally reversible, finite-rate coupled to its reservoirs, operated at the power level that
*maximizes power output* — not a bound on heat engines generally. GT-6's real design-point
efficiency (43.0% wet / 41.2% dry) already exceeds the CA value computed for the same reservoir
pair (38.6%/37.3%, chain C1). A plant engineered for efficiency, not power density, is not
described by the CA model, and the fact that real equipment already beats it is decisive, not
merely suggestive.

**What it ruled out:** The intuitive but incorrect move of treating "accounts for finite-rate heat
transfer" as the same thing as "is a valid ceiling." Finite-rate heat transfer is real and does
destroy exergy (this is exactly what GT-15's exergy-correct ceiling and chain C3's category (a)
and (b) brackets price in), but Curzon-Ahlborn prices it in for the wrong optimization target.

### Dead End: An exergy ceiling that bakes in current HX approach-temperature gaps and steam-metallurgy limits

**What was tried:** Following the question's third suggested candidate — constructing a
"law-permitted ceiling" that already incorporates the ≈28 °C salt-to-steam approach gap current
heat-exchanger design accepts, and the live-steam-temperature cap current turbine metallurgy
imposes, on the reasoning that these constraints are "unavoidable" in practice.

**Why abandoned:** Approach-temperature gaps and metallurgy limits are engineering and economic
conventions (current constraints, per the Assumptions Table's taxonomy), not laws — GT-6 itself
documents three different metallurgy/pressure classes (subcritical, supercritical,
ultrasupercritical) at three different approach gaps, all operating today or in near-term design
studies, which is direct evidence these limits move with investment and materials choice. Folding
a movable convention into "the ceiling" produces a number that looks rigorous but is actually
just a restatement of current best design practice — the same failure mode as citing
best-in-class incumbent practice as a theoretical limit, just with the incumbent figure computed
rather than observed.

**What it ruled out:** Treating "the ceiling" and "the best achievable design today" as the same
quantity. They are not: the first is what chain C1 computes (GT-15's exergy-correct bound), the
second is GT-6's design-point figure, and the distance between them is exactly chain C2's gap —
collapsing them would have made the central question of this analysis unanswerable by
definition.

### Dead End: Reporting the naive single-reservoir Carnot gap (≈19 points) as the headline figure

**What was tried:** Early in Phase 4, computing the gap as naive-Carnot-ceiling minus
current-practice (62.3% − 43.0% = 19.3 points), matching the treatment a prior theoretical-limit
pass on this same domain used.

**Why abandoned:** Once GT-15's exergy-correct derivation (chain C1) established that the salt's
own temperature glide lowers the correct ceiling by roughly 8 points, continuing to report the
naive 19-point figure as "the gap" would have attributed real, structural exergy content of the
heat source — exergy that no engine, however perfect, could ever have extracted, because it was
never thermodynamically available in the first place — to the plant's own shortfall. That
materially changes the headline relative-gap figure (≈21% vs. a prior ≈31%) and therefore the
answer to Part 5's recoverable/locked-in split.

**What it ruled out:** Any synthesis in §6 that quotes "~19 points" or "~31% relative" as the
gap. Both numbers are real and reported (chain C2's fifth hop, for direct comparability with
other treatments of this domain), but they are explicitly labeled as the looser, naive-ceiling
figures, not the headline result.

### Dead End: Resolving Crescent Dunes' and Gemasolar's exact cycle parameters from secondary sources

**What was tried:** Multiple WebSearch and WebFetch attempts to establish Crescent Dunes' and
Gemasolar's measured or design-point gross/net cycle efficiencies, including direct fetch
attempts against NREL's SolarPACES project database and NREL's SAM case-study documentation.

**Why abandoned:** Both direct-fetch attempts against nrel.gov subdomains (solarpaces.nrel.gov,
sam.nrel.gov) failed with DNS resolution errors, and the secondary sources that were reachable
disagree with each other: Wikipedia's Crescent Dunes figure ("almost 600 °C" hot tank) is
30–35 °C above the 565 °C-class design-basis literature this analysis otherwise relies on
(GT-4–GT-6), and no source reachable by this analysis — primary or secondary — states a measured
or design gross/net cycle efficiency for either plant.

**What it ruled out:** Presenting any specific percentage for Crescent Dunes or Gemasolar in §6.
The honest-depth path is naming this as a data gap (chain C2's final hop, GT-12?/GT-14?), not
estimating past it with a number dressed as a fact.

FP_EOF
echo done

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: The 290 °C cold salt tank as the cold reservoir

**What was tried:** Computing η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot using the two salt-tank temperatures
directly (565 °C hot tank, 290 °C cold tank) as the reservoir pair, since both are well-sourced,
round, and salient numbers (GT-4).

**Why abandoned:** The cold tank is the return leg of the heat *source* loop, not a heat sink —
nothing in the plant rejects waste heat at 290 °C. The arithmetic is well-formed (1 − 563/838 =
32.8%) but the result is not a ceiling on the actual machine: GT-6's real, operating design
practice (43.0% gross) already exceeds it. A bound real equipment exceeds has the wrong reservoir
pair, not a measurement error — this is the decisive test, and this framing fails it.

**What it ruled out:** Any later re-derivation that reaches for the tank pair because both
numbers are salt-side and convenient. The correct cold reservoir is always the point where the
*cycle* rejects heat (chain C1), never a temperature internal to the heat-delivery loop, however
tempting its availability.

### Dead End: Curzon-Ahlborn as the "more realistic" law-permitted ceiling

**What was tried:** Using η_CA = 1 − √(T_cold/T_hot) as the ceiling instead of (or alongside)
Carnot, on the reasoning offered in the question itself — that it "accounts for the unavoidable
finite-rate heat transfer needed to deliver nonzero power" and so is a tighter, more physically
honest bound than the classical, zero-power-limit Carnot figure.

**Why abandoned:** Curzon-Ahlborn is the efficiency of one specific, named engine model —
internally reversible, finite-rate coupled to its reservoirs, operated at the power level that
*maximizes power output* — not a bound on heat engines generally. GT-6's real design-point
efficiency (43.0% wet / 41.2% dry) already exceeds the CA value computed for the same reservoir
pair (38.6%/37.3%, chain C1). A plant engineered for efficiency, not power density, is not
described by the CA model, and the fact that real equipment already beats it is decisive, not
merely suggestive.

**What it ruled out:** The intuitive but incorrect move of treating "accounts for finite-rate heat
transfer" as the same thing as "is a valid ceiling." Finite-rate heat transfer is real and does
destroy exergy (this is exactly what GT-15's exergy-correct ceiling and chain C3's category (a)
and (b) brackets price in), but Curzon-Ahlborn prices it in for the wrong optimization target.

### Dead End: An exergy ceiling that bakes in current HX approach-temperature gaps and steam-metallurgy limits

**What was tried:** Following the question's third suggested candidate — constructing a
"law-permitted ceiling" that already incorporates the ≈28 °C salt-to-steam approach gap current
heat-exchanger design accepts, and the live-steam-temperature cap current turbine metallurgy
imposes, on the reasoning that these constraints are "unavoidable" in practice.

**Why abandoned:** Approach-temperature gaps and metallurgy limits are engineering and economic
conventions (current constraints, per the Assumptions Table's taxonomy), not laws — GT-6 itself
documents three different metallurgy/pressure classes (subcritical, supercritical,
ultrasupercritical) at three different approach gaps, all operating today or in near-term design
studies, which is direct evidence these limits move with investment and materials choice. Folding
a movable convention into "the ceiling" produces a number that looks rigorous but is actually
just a restatement of current best design practice — the same failure mode as citing
best-in-class incumbent practice as a theoretical limit, just with the incumbent figure computed
rather than observed.

**What it ruled out:** Treating "the ceiling" and "the best achievable design today" as the same
quantity. They are not: the first is what chain C1 computes (GT-15's exergy-correct bound), the
second is GT-6's design-point figure, and the distance between them is exactly chain C2's gap —
collapsing them would have made the central question of this analysis unanswerable by
definition.

### Dead End: Reporting the naive single-reservoir Carnot gap (≈19 points) as the headline figure

**What was tried:** Early in Phase 4, computing the gap as naive-Carnot-ceiling minus
current-practice (62.3% − 43.0% = 19.3 points), matching the treatment a prior theoretical-limit
pass on this same domain used.

**Why abandoned:** Once GT-15's exergy-correct derivation (chain C1) established that the salt's
own temperature glide lowers the correct ceiling by roughly 8 points, continuing to report the
naive 19-point figure as "the gap" would have attributed real, structural exergy content of the
heat source — exergy that no engine, however perfect, could ever have extracted, because it was
never thermodynamically available in the first place — to the plant's own shortfall. That
materially changes the headline relative-gap figure (≈21% vs. a prior ≈31%) and therefore the
answer to Part 5's recoverable/locked-in split.

**What it ruled out:** Any synthesis in §6 that quotes "~19 points" or "~31% relative" as the
gap. Both numbers are real and reported (chain C2's fifth hop, for direct comparability with
other treatments of this domain), but they are explicitly labeled as the looser, naive-ceiling
figures, not the headline result.

### Dead End: Resolving Crescent Dunes' and Gemasolar's exact cycle parameters from secondary sources

**What was tried:** Multiple WebSearch and WebFetch attempts to establish Crescent Dunes' and
Gemasolar's measured or design-point gross/net cycle efficiencies, including direct fetch
attempts against NREL's SolarPACES project database and NREL's SAM case-study documentation.

**Why abandoned:** Both direct-fetch attempts against nrel.gov subdomains (solarpaces.nrel.gov,
sam.nrel.gov) failed with DNS resolution errors, and the secondary sources that were reachable
disagree with each other: Wikipedia's Crescent Dunes figure ("almost 600 °C" hot tank) is
30–35 °C above the 565 °C-class design-basis literature this analysis otherwise relies on
(GT-4–GT-6), and no source reachable by this analysis — primary or secondary — states a measured
or design gross/net cycle efficiency for either plant.

**What it ruled out:** Presenting any specific percentage for Crescent Dunes or Gemasolar in §6.
The honest-depth path is naming this as a data gap (chain C2's final hop, GT-12?/GT-14?), not
estimating past it with a number dressed as a fact.

FP_EOF
echo done

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Cite the exergy-correct, non-isothermal-source Carnot ceiling —
**≈54.3% wet-cooled / ≈52.3% dry-cooled** — as the law-permitted ceiling, not the naive
single-reservoir Carnot figure (≈62.3%/60.6%, valid but loose) and not Curzon-Ahlborn (≈38.6%/
37.3%, not a valid ceiling at all — real design practice already exceeds it) (chain C1). Against
that ceiling, current commercial design practice (43.0% wet / 41.2% dry gross; an estimated
35.8–38.3% net after parasitics) sits roughly **11 points below on a gross basis (≈21% relative)
and 14–16 points below on a net basis (≈27–31% relative)** (chain C2) — a materially smaller gap
than the ≈19–25 points the naive Carnot figure would report, because the naive figure
overstates the ceiling by treating the salt as isothermal rather than as the cooling,
sensible-heat stream it actually is (chain C2). Of the ≈11-point gross gap, roughly **2–4
points (a quarter to a third) are recoverable with known near-term engineering** at the current
565 °C salt temperature (supercritical steam pressure, tighter HX approach, wet cooling where
water is available, better storage dispatch), while roughly **7–9 points (two-thirds to
three-quarters) are fundamentally locked in** by the Second Law applied to a real, finite-power
heat exchanger and real turbomachinery (chain C4). Raising the salt temperature (toward 650 °C
nitrate-salt ultrasupercritical steam, or beyond via chloride-salt/sCO₂ designs) is a separate,
substantial lever on *absolute* efficiency, not a way to close this fixed-T_hot gap — and on the
one case this analysis could compute, it narrows the *relative* gap too (≈12% at 650 °C against
≈21% at 565 °C) (chain C4).

**Key insight:** The question "which ceiling is defensible" is not a preliminary to this
analysis — it is most of the analysis. Molten salt is not an isothermal reservoir; it is a
finite stream that cools 275 °C while delivering heat, and a Carnot ceiling computed at its peak
temperature silently assumes away roughly 8 points of "headroom" that was never thermodynamically
available to begin with (chain C1). Correcting for this shrinks the apparent gap by nearly half
in relative terms (≈21% vs. a naive ≈31%) and, more importantly, inverts the naive intuition that
"raising T_hot closes the Carnot gap": raising T_hot resets the whole bracket upward and, if
anything, makes the cycle *more* reversible relative to its own new ceiling, but it does not
touch the locked-in component of the gap at the original operating point at all (chain C4).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This synthesis accepts a wide, explicitly stated uncertainty band on
the gap decomposition (chain C3, LOW confidence) in exchange for not inventing false precision: no
plant-specific exergy/heat-and-mass-balance model for a molten-salt tower was located, so
categories (a), (b), (c)'s residual, and the cycling portion of (e) are Fermi brackets, not
measurements (chain C3). It also accepts a genuine, named data gap on Crescent Dunes' and
Gemasolar's actual cycle parameters rather than filling it with numbers dressed as facts (chain
C2) — no chain — flagged assumption only. Finally, it deliberately leaves the economic question
of whether the locked-in and recoverable efficiency figures are worth pursuing at all, given
competing dispatchable-generation cost trajectories, as a named but unquantified second-order
channel (chain C5) rather than folding an unsupported claim into the headline numbers.

**Pre-check:** head C1 (MEDIUM), C2 (MEDIUM), C3 (LOW), C4 (LOW) · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: LOW · Inputs ceiling: LOW
**Confidence:** LOW — the headline recoverable/locked-in split (chain C4) is capped by chain C3's
LOW rating, which is itself capped by the Fermi-bracket apportionment (A-9, A-10) rather than a
plant-specific exergy model. This is not a weak conclusion in the sense of being poorly
reasoned — chains C1 and C2, which establish *which* ceiling is defensible and *how large* the
gap is, are both MEDIUM and rest on read-at-source primary documents (Sandia SAND2011-9320,
SAND2002-0120, the DOE SunShot fact sheet) — it is LOW specifically on the *apportionment* of the
gap across mechanisms, which is the one piece of Part 4 that would need a per-component
exergy-destruction study or a measured commercial-scale operating record to tighten, exactly as
chain C3's own confidence line states. The direction of every finding here (ceiling choice, gap
size, dominance of the locked-in component, T_hot as a separate lever) is robust to that
remaining uncertainty; only the precise point-estimates within the 2–4 / 7–9 split would move.

FP_EOF
echo done

names and flags; C2's confidence line already prices this in.

nothing in this analysis settles it, because no measured commercial-scale figure was located

without necessarily raising T_hot) might imply" — ruled out directly by C1's GT-15 floor argument

no cited roadmap figure in this analysis's sources achieves the exergy-correct ceiling at fixed
T_hot), so this rival does not survive.

ceiling is not the right figure to cite, the ~11/14-16 point gap is not the right size, and the
~2-4 / ~7-9 recoverable/locked-in split is not the right split.

   percentages are computed against, so C1's "same Q-basis as GT-6" claim is wrong.

   ~12% relative" finding does not hold.
3. (economist/skeptic) GT-6's figures are unvalidated case-study projections (A-6); real
   commercial towers could underperform design by many points, making the true current-practice
   gap much larger than C2 reports and the locked-in share understated, because unmeasured
   operational losses outside categories (a)-(e) could dominate.

   losses much smaller than category (a)'s bracket assumes, or temperature-glide mismatch could
   be a much larger factor in molten-salt steam generators specifically than generic Rankine-cycle
   regularities suggest.

   parasitic ratio onto a modern 100+ MW design; a modern plant's actual parasitic profile
   (different pump/VFD/cooling technology at a different scale) could differ enough to invalidate

- **Cluster B — Design-figure external validity and independence** (causes 3, 7): bears on C2,

- **Cluster C — Apportionment/estimate reliability** (causes 4, 5, 6): bears on C3, C4, A-8, A-9.
  This is the same weakness C3/C4's own `**Confidence:**` lines already name as the cause of
  their LOW rating.
- **Cluster D — Unmodeled reliability/availability losses** (cause 8): bears on C2's data-gap
  hop and GT-12?, but names a loss channel **outside** categories (a)-(e) entirely — the sharpest
  finding of this pass.

**Disposition.**
- Cluster A — accepted risk, mitigation already in place: A-11 is already named as an explicit,
  unconfirmed caveat on C3's 650 °C figure and on C3's `**Confidence:**` line; no further plan
  change needed beyond what is already disclosed.
- Cluster B — accepted risk, named mitigation: the "independently corroborated" framing in C2
  should be read as *consistent-across-two-documents*, not as fully independent confirmation,
  since both may share a common Sandia-analysis lineage; this does not change either chain's
  numeric content, since GT-6 and GT-8 already agree to within 0.2 points regardless of
  independence, but it tempers how much epistemic weight that agreement should carry.
- Cluster C — accepted risk, mitigation already in place: this is the dominant, already-disclosed
  driver of C3/C4's LOW rating, with the verification path (a per-component exergy-destruction
  model, or a measured commercial-scale operating record) already named on both chains'
  `**Confidence:**` lines; no further action beyond what §4 and §6 already state.
- Cluster D — **plan change**: this pass surfaced a loss channel the five-category decomposition
  does not cover. §6's `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` line has been updated to name this scope
  boundary explicitly (reliability/availability losses are real, additive, and unquantified here)
  rather than leaving the five-category decomposition looking exhaustive when it is not.

**Falsification.** The conclusion is false if a verified, plant-specific exergy/heat-and-mass
balance for an operating commercial-scale (>50 MW) molten-salt tower shows the recoverable share
of the ~11-point gross gap to be the majority rather than the minority (i.e., shows categories
(a)-(c) are mostly closeable with known engineering rather than mostly a Second-Law floor), or if
GT-15's exergy-ceiling derivation is shown to use integration bounds inconsistent with how
GT-6's cycle-efficiency figures are actually computed.

FP_EOF

For those limbs the criterion quotes the analysis text directly; the scan is quoted only where the band is determined by what its columns cover.

Do not re-perform the scan to fill a missing table; a missing or incomplete scan is itself the evidence to score against.
78	
79	Verifying the scan is present and internally coherent is not verifying its rows are correct — a row's finding is checked against the analysis text by a reader, and no gate in this tree scores a live run's compliance.
80	
81	**Precedence rule (no double-counting):** A single observable defect can match the
82	descriptor of more than one criterion — for example, an unverified ground truth used in a
83	chain without the `?` suffix is named by Criteria 2, 3, and 5. When this happens, band the
84	defect under the **lowest-numbered criterion** whose descriptor names it, and merely *note*
85	the overlap under the other criteria without lowering their band for the same underlying
86	problem. One real flaw must not independently drag down two or three criteria, because that
87	would let a single defect trip the hand-wavy cap on its own.

91	## Exceptions Summary
92	
93	Three conditions relax the HIGH-confidence requirements introduced into Criteria 3 and 5.
94	This section is a navigation aid, listing them together for quick reference; where its
95	wording differs from the per-criterion clause, the per-criterion clause governs.
96	
97	**(a) Unreachable source** — Criterion 3. A ground truth cites a source the Phase 3
98	verification step could not open; the Phase 3 failure record naming which source and why
99	unreachable is the satisfying evidence; the ground truth may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains.
100	
101	**(b) Speculative chain** — Criterion 5. A chain is explicitly marked speculative and the
102	analysis states the claim it supports is not load-bearing; the mark plus that statement is
103	the satisfying evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM. Its confidence line still gives each of
104	its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account of why no available
105	evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason. A speculative chain cited on
106	another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer qualifies. A speculative chain with no
107	verification path is therefore not cited on another chain's head; it stays speculative or
108	moves to Abandoned Reasoning.
109	
110	**(c) Absent-fails derivation** — Criterion 5. A chain establishes that a conclusion does not
111	follow from an assumption shown to be false; the named false assumption is the satisfying
112	evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM.
113	
114	An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one names it in the relevant
115	verdict block and cites the required evidence; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the
116	analysis's behalf.

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")
179

182	## Verdict Block Format
183	
184	The six verdict blocks are emitted together under the single top-level heading
185	`## Self-Audit Gate (process output)`, one `##` heading holding all six in criterion order —
186	the same placement the adversarial pass record and the self-audit scan prescribe for themselves.
187	They are one artifact, not six; nesting them beneath another section's heading makes them a
188	subsection of something they do not belong to, and a reader or a check keyed to that heading
189	must find it in the same structural position on every run.
190	
191	Each of the 6 criteria requires exactly one verdict block. Use the standard form when the
192	analysis section exists and contains scoreable content:
193	
194	```text
195	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
196	Quoted span: "[Direct quote of the specific text that most directly determines the band assigned — from the analysis being scored, or, per the admission below, from the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6 or the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2, each emitted as process output for this analysis.]"
197	Band: [**Rigorous** / **Sound** / **Hand-wavy** / **Absent**]
198	Justification: [One sentence tying the quoted span to the observable descriptor for
199	that band — name the specific structural property present or absent.]
200	```
201	
202	The self-audit scan and the Assumption Audit scan are not output sections, and they are the only artifacts outside the six-section analysis a verdict block may quote: the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6, and the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2. Every other criterion quotes the analysis text itself, and the §6→§4 closure ledger is admitted nowhere — it is a drafting artifact that describes a document other than the one being scored.
203	
204	Use the gap-citation form when the criterion scores Absent because the section or named
205	artifact is missing or empty — in that case there is no span to quote, and the documented
206	absence is the evidence:
207	
208	```text
209	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
210	Gap: [Name what is missing and where it should have appeared — e.g., "No Derivation
211	Chains section exists; chains of the form 'GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate] → [conclusion]'
212	should appear in section 4 (Derivation Chains) for each conclusion stated in section 6
213	(Conclusion)."]
214	Band: Absent
215	Justification: [One sentence: the absence itself is the structural failure that triggers
216	the gate — the criterion cannot be scored against a non-existent artifact.]
217	```
218	
219	Verdict blocks (not a consolidated table) are required because each block contains a quoted
220	span or a gap citation. Without that span, the evidence-quoting requirement cannot be audited:
221	a summary table of band labels can be produced by asserting compliance, but a verdict block
222	containing a quote that contradicts its claimed band creates a contradiction that cannot be
223	sustained.
